title: Abandoning
hookLine: five ways with a bad thought: replace it, see its danger, ignore it, calm its cause, and at last suppress it (MN 20)

cards: Some thoughts get past the gate anyway. You're lying in bed and the argument from lunch starts replaying. Or a craving that won't quit.
Or a worry, looping like a song you can't stand. Just let it go is easy advice to give. It rarely comes with instructions.
The Buddha gave some: five ways, in order, from gentlest to strongest, each with its own picture. The first one is a carpenter's trick.

teach.h: A FINER PEG FOR A COARSE ONE.
teach.b: The sutta, in the Middle Length Discourses, is named for the stilling of thoughts. Way one: when an unwholesome thought keeps coming, turn the mind to another sign, one connected with the wholesome.

If it's anger, kindness. If it's craving, something that cools it. Like a skilled carpenter, the Buddha says, who knocks out a coarse peg with a finer one: you drive a better peg in, and it pushes the old one through.
Way two: look at the danger in the thought. Where is this taking me? He compares it to a young person fond of finery, horrified to find a carcass hung around their neck.
Way three: simply don't attend to it, like someone who closes their eyes or looks away. Way four: calm the thought's momentum, like a man walking fast who asks, why am I hurrying?

He slows down, then stands, then sits, then lies down. Way five, the last resort: teeth clenched, tongue pressed to the roof of the mouth, hold the mind down with the mind, like a strong man pinning a weaker one.
Force comes last, not first. It's tempting to start at way five, and that's the one that wears a person out.
Look back at the week: blameless is best, four parts, work is practice, enough, four efforts, guard the gate, and today, a finer peg.

how: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist schools teach these five methods for working with persistent thoughts, often recommending the gentler ones first and keeping forceful suppression for emergencies.

o: walking away from home to become a monk
letting go of harmful thoughts already here
emptying the mind of every single thought

games.q: the five ways: tap the pairs.
p: a fine peg knocks out a coarse one

s: MN 20 starts by forcing the thought down
force is the fifth and last way; the first is replacing it with something wholesome.
one of the ways is simply not paying attention to the thought
the third way: like looking away from what you don't want to see.
the five ways are meant to be tried in order, gentlest first
each is offered if the one before hasn't worked.

games.q: an angry thought about a coworker keeps coming back. by MN 20, what's the first thing to try?
o: clench your teeth and push it down.
turn to a wholesome thought, like kindness, in its place.
replay the argument until it's settled.
games.why: the first way is the carpenter's: replace the coarse peg with a finer one. force is kept for last.

practice: Let a small, sticky thought come up, nothing overwhelming, and notice what kind it is: irritation, craving, worry.
Then choose its finer peg, that person on a good day, the cool, complete breath, one thing that's fine right now, and gently drive it in, letting it push the old one through.

wordCard.voice: Abandoning. The second effort: letting go of unwholesome thoughts already here. The sutta gives five ways, gentlest first.

orig.note: Pali pahāna: abandoning, letting go, the second of the four right efforts.

carryVoice: Your line: a finer peg. Force comes last, never first. Three hundred eighty-five days, and a week done.
